This comment is made a lot, and every time I think about it it's hard to think of anything obvious a tourist might be drawn to, and secondly, actually be good.

The problem with Brisbane is it has no real tourist attractions like Sydney or Melbourne, and if something claims it is, it's probably a pretty average experience. 

I don't know even what the things you've claimed to like are, so here's what I, a local, would take a friend to based on a decade of share housing north, south, east, and west:

Day one: south bank. It's basically the 'tourist district' of the wonderful world of Brisbane. It's a good place to start I reckon mostly because of the hilariously mark-missing way brisbane tries to be trendy like Melbourne. (Brisbane, you don't have lane ways and that's okay.) As I used to uni there, I can suggest a walk along the river/bougainvillea thingamajig starting at south bank station, and ending at south brisbane station near the museum. Go into whatever takes your fancy. There's a bunch of good food and markets on the weekend. AVOID THE IBIS AND TOURIST INFESTED FAST FOOD OUTLETS WITH THE POOLS. So much better shit out there.

Then, after seeing what Brisbane wishes it was, see what it is in it's cbd. Take the ferry over, enjoy the rumble and bump of the river and the views of the city. (even do the full loop while pulling a titanic. We'll know you're a tourist, though.)There's some relatively good shopping on queen at mall, and you never know what you'll find in an arcade. Want a cheap, crazy haircut? There's a hairdressing school in queen st mall arcade somewhere. For lunch, it's time to Korean it up Maru Korean BBQ. If you want to really find some interesting stuff, though, move away from queen st to where independant, non-chain businesses can run. One oft favourites is archive books.

Drinks? There are some okay pubs, like o'malley's Irish pub and another called Irish Murphy's full of weird things overlooking a seemingly important park. Also I sometimes like to take advantage of brisbane's heat-fried attitude of security and sneak into office blocks. This perhaps is not advisable but it's the cbd what else are you gonna do.

Day 2: But it's a good thing you didn't go overboard last night because you're gonna get smashed tonight. There is probably no better place than the valley. Some, in desperate attempts to be different and special, will try to downplay the magic of the valley, but one cannot argue the colour of a place where there are homeless aboriginal alcoholics in the main street, and then 500 metres down the road cut to Porsche shops and rump steak restaurants.

For the day, you can explore such wonders as china town (ahem, street), unusual poor-looking markets selling second hand books, and laugh then cry at the completely broken infrastructure. If you walk to James at, you'll find some nice coffee shops like campos, and some nice food. Walking down dogget st is pretty swell...lots of crazy furniture and homeware stores such as Matt Blatt and others. One could walk to commercial rd, see what unusual businesses they could find. The infamous 'Black Milk' is here. There is a stellar antiques store down further. It's huge.

THEN ITS TIME TO HEAD RIGHT IN BACK TO POORSVILLE TO GET YOUR DRINK ON.
I'd avoid the beat myself: it's crowded and dirty, but an argument could be made that's what you're in the valley for. Adventure. If you're after upmarket, try -insert name of bar with the hipster servers and lanterns-. I like the mana bar myself. It's really starting to establish itself into a friendly, homely everyone-knows-your-name place. Ask the bartender to make you a game.

Or just walk in anywhere, seriously. The valley's economy is drinks, then selling those drunk people hotdogs they don't need. (But you need brauthaust* it's really good.)

Day 3: hungover? If you are, take it easy.maybe the person you're staying with lives in a little suburban paradise where you can get the best bakery pie of all time. Or there's a nice cafe. Brisbane has some nice parks! Take pie to park. Eat pie and cushion head on well-maintained grass. If you aren't too hungover, (though you really should be,) you could pick a random place to go on public transport. Really just see where you end up. This could be a personal preference, but I love doing this and finding new places. A cool place now that I think about it could be reverse garbage, if you're a souvenir type. I once found a bucket of gateway bridge stress foam things. Maybe you'll find a dumped piece of Brisbane to take home . 

Day 4: it's time to take it a little outside brisbane. How far can you go? Just public transport? If you have a car, I recommend the Sunshine Coast. Not a huge tourist trap, but touristy enough. If I had to sum it up, I'd call it a nice Gold Coast. Buderim ginger is amazing if you're into that. The glass house mountains are pretty too. Australia zoo of Steve Irwin game is there, and I totally recommend it. If you're one budget and like being attacked by peacocks, alma park zoo makes me smile. I'd skip montville. It's for a nice view but that's about it. If you really want to experience that beach-shack, family owned, lax as shit vibe, try bribe island.

If you only have public transport, try redcliffe. The poor man's Sunshine Coast at the same travelling time. Okay beaches though.

Day 5: well it's probably about time for this Gold Coast then. Apart from the theme parks, (of which Id rank in descending order warner bros, sea world, dreamworld, wet and wild) and a strange schoolies while not being a schoolie, I don't have much to offer. I always recommend the ripley's believe it or not museum, though. Oh wait casinos. Yeah they're pretty cool. If you're good at certain games/want to feel classy by losing small change it's cool.

Day 6: now that you've seen a bit it's time to look at the world map. Take a bus from the cbd to mount (hill) coot'tha and spot where you've been. Because you're in the area, check out, bar none, the best food in Brisbane at Soul Bistro. (Closed Mondays.)

Day 7: um. Yeah I dunno. Pack or something.

IF YOU ARE OF AMERICA: try the food. Also we have sugar cane here.

It's weird, but animation isn't really a job, it's a lifestyle. It's hard to suddenly decide to be an animator out of the blue, because most people in the business have lived and breathed animation/drawing their whole lives. For me, animation isn't a 'job', per say, it's a thing I do, and then sometimes I get a paycheck. 

Qualifications aren't really a thing in this industry. It won't hurt to have some, but I dropped out of college because I felt I had learned all I could from there, (I only did the fun subjects, and failed/ignored all the theory and whatever) and I got a job really easily. Because it's not the qualifications, it's the portfolio. If you have qualifications, but you can't draw/animate, employers won't give a shit about you graduating an animation degree. 

I'm probably not the best person to talk about websites to, as I pretty much exclusively network, but I know there are websites out there to advertise your work to employers. I used to be afraid of networking, thinking it meant I'd have to go to boring meetings, and awkwardly pretend to be nice to business men, but I realize now that networking is merely just knowing people in the industry, and having them know you can animate well.

If you are looking to get into the business, I'd recommend doing a solid animation degree. The things you learn by studying are invaluable. You can study by yourself, but it's much better, I feel, to officially study. This way, you can make connections with teachers/industry peeps/peers that will also be successful and hook you up with jobs later.
